meta.blurb: A stolen letter could ruin a great lady, and the police of Paris have searched for months without finding it. Only Dupin thinks like the clever thief who took it. Can he win a battle of wits with a dangerous minister?
meta.bible: C. Auguste Dupin: a Parisian gentleman of great intelligence who solves mysteries by thinking as the criminal thinks; calm, dry-humoured, fond of the dark and of his pipe. Narrator: Dupin's unnamed friend, who tells the story in the first person. Prefect G: the head of the Paris police, thorough but unimaginative, who laughs at Dupin's ideas. Minister D: a bold, clever and unprincipled politician, both poet and mathematician, who steals the letter. The lady: a royal personage and the rightful owner of the letter; the third person is the royal person from whom she wishes to hide it. Paris: where the story takes place, on an autumn evening. Rue Dunôt: Dupin's street, number 33, third floor, in the Faubourg St Germain. Neapolitans: the Minister's servants, easily made drunk. Abernethy: a famous physician in Dupin's joke. Vienna: where the Minister once did Dupin an evil turn. Crébillon: author of the French play Atrée, from which Dupin copies two lines; Atreus and Thyestes: the brothers in that old tale. Reward: fifty thousand francs, later doubled. Facts: the Minister swapped a similar letter on the lady's table; the letter is hidden in plain view in a card-rack under the mantelpiece, turned inside out; Dupin makes a copy with a bread seal and a staged street disturbance. Voice and tone: calm, clever and dry; a detective tale told in the first person by a friend, with a twist of humour; no violence.

A1A2: On a windy autumn evening in Paris, I sat with my friend Dupin.
Suddenly the door opened, and the head of the Paris police came in.
Dupin did not light the lamp, because he liked thinking in the dark.
The Prefect said the problem was simple, but he could not solve it.
A very important paper had been stolen from the royal rooms.
If the wrong person read it, the lady would suffer greatly.
The lady was reading it alone when someone came into the room.
The Minister saw the letter, and he quickly swapped it for another.
When he left, he took her letter, and she could say nothing.
For months the Minister has used the letter to gain power.
The letter must be in the Minister's house, because he had been searched.
The Prefect said the Minister was a poet, so he was almost a fool.
For three months, the police searched the Minister's house every night.
The police opened every drawer and looked for secret places.
They pushed long needles into the chairs and took off table tops.
They looked at every joint of the furniture through a microscope.
They looked in the beds, behind the mirrors, and under the carpets.
The police numbered each part of the house and searched them all.
The garden had bricks, but nobody had touched the moss.
The police turned every page of every book in the library.
They searched under the carpets, behind the paper, and in the cellars.
The Prefect asked for advice, but he left the room sad.
A month later, the Prefect came back and was still unhappy.
Dupin told a story about a doctor and a rich, mean man.
Dupin asked for a cheque, and then he would give the letter.
The Prefect signed the cheque, took his letter, and ran away.
Dupin said that the police had done their work well.
A little boy always won the game of even and odd.
The boy guessed by thinking about how clever his friend was.
The boy copied his friend's face, and then he knew his thoughts.
The police thought that everyone hides things the way they do.
The Minister is both a poet and a mathematician, so he thinks well.
The Minister knew the police would search, so he hid the letter simply.
Dupin remembered the Prefect's laugh and put on green glasses.
The Minister acted bored, while Dupin looked around the room.
On the table lay papers and books, but nothing seemed strange.
Under the fireplace hung a dirty card-rack with a torn letter.
That letter looked very different from the one the Prefect described.
The dirt and the tear made Dupin think it was a trick.
Dupin saw that the old letter had been turned inside out.
Next day, a loud bang outside made the Minister run to the window.
Dupin took the letter and left a copy in its place.
The noise in the street was made by a man Dupin had paid.
Dupin did not take the letter at once, because it was dangerous.
Dupin wanted to help the lady and ruin the Minister's plans.
Dupin felt no pity for the Minister, who would soon fall.
Dupin wished he could see the Minister open the letter.
Dupin wrote a short message inside, for the Minister to find.
Dupin copied two lines from an old French play.
The best hiding place was the plainest one of all.
B1B2: On a gusty autumn evening in Paris, I am sitting with my friend Dupin in his small library on the third floor. We have smoked our pipes in silence for an hour, watching the smoke curl through the dark.
Just then the door is thrown open, and the Prefect of the Paris police walks in. We have not seen him for several years, but we welcome him warmly, for he is an amusing man in his own way.

Dupin gets up to light a lamp, but he sits down again when he hears that the matter needs thought. He says that a hard problem is best studied in the dark, and the Prefect laughs and calls this another of his odd ideas.
The Prefect says that the case is very simple, and yet it has puzzled everyone completely. Dupin answers that perhaps the mystery is a little too plain, and the Prefect bursts out laughing.

The Prefect begs us to keep the matter secret, because he might lose his post if it were known. A very important paper has been stolen from the royal rooms, and the thief is known, because he was seen taking it.
The paper is a letter, and it would bring shame on a very important lady if a certain person saw it. Whoever holds it therefore has great power over her, and he can use it in politics.
The lady was alone in her room, reading the letter, when another important person suddenly walked in. She did not want him to see it, so she dropped it on a table with the address facing upward.
The Minister's sharp eyes saw the letter at once, and he knew the handwriting and the lady's fear. He took out a letter of his own that looked much the same and laid it beside hers.
When he leaves, the Minister quietly takes the lady's letter and leaves his own on the table. She sees what he does, but she cannot say a word, because the other person is standing right beside her.

For months the Minister has used his power to gain advantages in politics, and the lady grows more desperate every day. She cannot ask for the letter openly, so she has begged the Prefect to find it secretly, and the reward is huge.

The letter must be close at hand, because the Minister may need to use it or destroy it quickly. The police had even arranged for him to be stopped twice in the street by pretend robbers, but they found nothing on him.

The Prefect says that the Minister is not quite a fool, but that he is a poet, which is almost the same thing. Dupin thoughtfully agrees, adding with a smile that he has written some poor poetry himself.

The Prefect describes how he searched the Minister's house in secret for three months, almost every night. The Minister often stays out all night, and his servants, who mostly come from Naples, are easily made drunk.

The Prefect says that his men opened every drawer in the house, and that no secret drawer could escape a trained police agent. Each cabinet was measured, because any extra space would have shown that something was hidden inside.

After the cabinets, the police turned to the chairs, and they pushed fine needles deep into every cushion. They also took the tops off the tables, because a letter can be hidden inside a hollow table leg.

I asked whether a hollow could not be found by tapping, and the Prefect explained that cotton wool stops any sound. So the police checked the rung of every chair, and every joint of the furniture, with a powerful microscope.
I asked whether they had looked behind the mirrors and inside the beds, and the Prefect said that of course they had. They had also checked the bedclothes, the curtains and the carpets.

The police divided the whole surface of the house into numbered squares, so that none could be missed. Then they examined every square inch under the microscope, and they did the same in the two houses next door.
The grounds around the house are all paved with brick, so they gave the police little trouble. They examined the moss between the bricks, and it was undisturbed.

The Prefect says they opened every package and paper, and turned over every page of every book, instead of just shaking them. They measured the thickness of each cover, and probed some new bindings with needles.
The police also took up the carpets and examined the floorboards, and they checked the paper on the walls. They even looked in the cellars, but nothing was found anywhere.

The Prefect admits that he may have made a mistake, and he asks what Dupin would advise. Dupin tells him to search the house again, but the Prefect is sure the letter is not there, and he leaves depressed.
About a month later the Prefect visits us again, and we find him in his usual chair. He has searched the hotel again, as Dupin advised, but it was wasted work, and the reward has now been doubled.
Dupin tells a story about a famous doctor named Abernethy. A rich miser once pretended to ask about a friend's illness to get free advice, and the doctor told him to take advice.

The Prefect says that he would gladly pay fifty thousand francs for good advice, and that he means it. Dupin opens a drawer, takes out a cheque book, and says that he will hand over the letter as soon as the cheque is signed.
At last the Prefect picks up a pen and signs the cheque for fifty thousand francs. Dupin puts it in his wallet, unlocks a desk, and gives him the letter, and the Prefect rushes out without a word.
When the Prefect has gone, Dupin begins to explain. He says that the police are very able and their search was perfect, but their methods did not suit this man.

Dupin tells of a schoolboy of about eight who won all the marbles at his school at a game called even and odd. One player holds some marbles in his closed hand, and the other must guess whether the number is even or odd.
The boy studied each opponent to see how clever he was. A simple player would probably switch from even to odd, but a cleverer one would see this coming and would not switch.
I said that this was only a matter of fitting your own mind to your opponent's. Dupin agreed, and said the boy copied his opponent's face and then waited to see what thoughts came into his own mind.

Dupin says that the police fail because they think only about how they themselves would hide a letter. When the reward grows larger, they search harder in the same old way instead of trying something new.
The Prefect decided the Minister was a fool because the man is known as a poet. But I said the Minister had also written about mathematics, and Dupin replied that he is both, and so he reasons well.

Dupin knew that the Minister was a courtier and a bold schemer who would expect the police to search his house. He thought that the Minister's nights out were tricks to help the police, and that the letter would be hidden simply.
Dupin reminds me how the Prefect laughed when he said the mystery was too plain. Then he put on a pair of green spectacles and went to visit the Minister, as if by chance, one fine morning.

Dupin finds the Minister yawning and lounging, and pretending to be bored, although he is really a very energetic man. Dupin complains about his weak eyes, and behind his spectacles he quietly studies the whole room.
Dupin looks carefully at the large writing-table where the Minister sits. Letters, papers, a few books and one or two musical instruments lie in confusion on it, but he sees nothing suspicious.

At last Dupin's eyes fall on a cheap cardboard card-rack, hanging by a dirty blue ribbon from a brass knob under the mantelpiece. It holds a few visiting cards and one letter, which is dirty, crumpled and torn nearly in two.

The letter in the rack has a large black seal and is addressed to the Minister in a small woman's hand. The stolen letter had a small red seal and a bold address, so it looks quite different, although the size matches.

Dupin thought the extreme difference was suspicious, and so were the dirt and the tear, which did not suit the Minister's neat habits. The letter was also in full view of every visitor, so Dupin kept the Minister talking about a subject he loved.

Looking at the edges of the paper, Dupin sees that they are more worn than they should be. Stiff paper wears like this when it is refolded the opposite way, so the letter has been turned inside out and readdressed.

The next morning Dupin comes back for his snuff-box, and the two men talk eagerly as before. Suddenly there is a loud bang like a pistol shot in the street below, followed by screams, and the Minister rushes to the window.

While the Minister is looking out of the window, Dupin steps over to the rack and takes the letter. He puts it in his pocket, and leaves in its place a copy which he made at home, using bread to make the seal.

The disturbance in the street was made by a man with a musket, who had fired it among a crowd of women and children. There was no bullet in it, and the man was paid by Dupin, so he was allowed to go his way.

I ask why Dupin did not simply seize the letter on his first visit and leave. Dupin says the Minister is a desperate man with devoted servants, and if he had tried, he might never have left the room alive.
Dupin says he has another reason, because he is on the side of the lady. The Minister does not know that the letter is gone, so he will go on using his power over her, and that will ruin him.
Dupin says that the Minister's fall will be sudden and awkward, because it is easier to climb up than to come down. He has no pity for the Minister, who is a clever man without any principles.
Dupin confesses that he would like to know what the Minister thinks when he must open the letter in the card-rack. I ask whether Dupin put anything special inside it.

It did not seem right to leave the inside of the letter blank, Dupin says, because that would have been insulting. The Minister once did him an evil turn in Vienna, and Dupin promised, in a good-humoured way, that he would remember it.

The words Dupin copied are two lines from a French play called Atrée, by Crébillon. They say that a plan so terrible, if not worthy of Atreus, is worthy of Thyestes, so the Minister will know who wrote them.

So the stolen letter went back to its owner, while the Prefect had searched every hidden corner of the house for months. The letter had been in plain sight the whole time, and it was a clever mind that found it, and not a careful one.
C1C2: It was a gusty autumn evening in Paris, and I was sitting with my friend Dupin in his small book-closet on the third floor, savouring the twin pleasures of thought and a good pipe. For a full hour neither of us had spoken, and anyone looking in would have taken us for two men wholly absorbed in the curling smoke. In truth my mind was elsewhere, turning over the strange cases that Dupin and I had discussed earlier that evening.

I was still thinking of those old mysteries when the door of the room was flung open and our old acquaintance, the Prefect of the Parisian police, strode in. We had not seen him for years, and we greeted him heartily, for he was a man in whom the comical and the contemptible lived in about equal parts. He had come, he told us, to ask the opinion of my friend on an official matter that had caused him a great deal of trouble.

Dupin rose to light the lamp, yet he sat down again the moment he learned that the visitor wanted his opinion, remarking that a problem which demands reflection is better examined in the dark. The Prefect, who had a habit of calling oddities everything he could not understand, replied that this was yet another of Dupin's strange notions. Dupin only agreed politely, handed his guest a pipe, and rolled a comfortable chair towards him.

The business was simple, the Prefect declared, so simple that he had no doubt his own men could manage it, and yet it had baffled them all utterly. Dupin suggested calmly that it might be the very simplicity of the thing that put him at fault, and that the mystery was perhaps a little too plain, a little too self-evident. At this the Prefect roared with laughter and protested that Dupin would be the death of him yet.

He first warned us, in the gravest tone, that the affair demanded absolute secrecy and that he would probably lose his position if it ever became known that he had confided in anyone. A document of the highest importance, he told us, had been stolen from the royal apartments, and the identity of the thief was beyond doubt, since he had been seen in the very act. It was equally certain, he added, that the paper was still in the thief's possession.

The document, the Prefect explained with the pomposity he reserved for diplomacy, gave its holder a certain power in a certain quarter where such power was enormously valuable. Were the letter shown to a particular third person, the honour of a lady of exalted rank would be called into question, and this gave the holder an ascendancy over her. The thief, he revealed, was the Minister D, a man who dared everything, whether becoming or unbecoming to a gentleman.

The lady had received the letter while she was alone in the royal boudoir, and she was reading it when she was interrupted by the entrance of the very person from whom she most wished to hide it. After one hurried and unsuccessful attempt to push it into a drawer, she was forced to leave it lying open on a table, with the address uppermost and the contents therefore unseen. At that moment, as ill luck would have it, the Minister D walked in.

His sharp eye fell on the letter immediately; he recognised the handwriting of the address, noticed the lady's confusion, and understood her whole secret in an instant. After finishing some official business in his usual brisk manner, he drew from his pocket a letter that resembled hers, opened it, pretended to read it, and set it down close beside the other. He then chatted about public affairs for a quarter of an hour, as calmly as if nothing were happening.

At last, in taking his leave, he picked up the letter to which he had no claim and walked out, leaving his own harmless one on the table. Its rightful owner watched him do it, yet she dared not call attention to the theft with the third person standing at her elbow. In this way the Minister gained exactly what he needed to make his power over her complete.

For some months, the Prefect explained, the Minister had wielded this power for political ends to a dangerous extent, and the unhappy lady was more convinced with every passing day that the letter must be recovered. Since it could not be demanded openly, she had in despair entrusted the matter to him, and the reward for success, he confided, was enormous. Dupin, wrapped in a whirlwind of smoke, remarked that no more sagacious agent could possibly be imagined, and the Prefect accepted the compliment with perfect gravity.

Dupin observed that the letter had to be kept ready to hand, since the Minister might need to produce it or destroy it at a moment's notice, and so it was surely hidden somewhere in his own house. The Prefect agreed, adding that the Minister had twice been waylaid by apparent footpads and thoroughly searched under his own supervision, without the smallest result. Dupin remarked drily that a man who was no fool must have foreseen such an ambush.

The Minister was not altogether a fool, the Prefect conceded, but he was a poet, which in his opinion was only one step removed from folly. Dupin, after a long and thoughtful draw on his meerschaum, replied that this was true enough, although he had himself been guilty of a little bad verse. I could not tell whether he was mocking the Prefect or himself, and I suspect that he was doing both.

The Prefect declared that he had taken his time and searched everywhere, for he held keys that would open any door in Paris, and for three months he had scarcely missed a night ransacking the Minister's hotel. The Minister was often away until morning, and his servants, mostly Neapolitans, slept far from his rooms and were easily made drunk. His honour was at stake, he added, and the reward, which he would not name, was enormous.

The furniture came first, the Prefect explained, and every drawer was opened, since no properly trained agent can be fooled by a secret drawer when a certain bulk of space must be accounted for in every cabinet. His men worked by accurate rules, and the fiftieth part of a line could not have escaped them. It was precisely the kind of thoroughness, I thought, of which he was proudest.

After the cabinets they took the chairs, he went on, and the cushions were probed with the long, fine needles that I had often seen him use. The tops were lifted from the tables as well, since a man wishing to hide something may remove the top, hollow out a leg, slip the object inside, and put the top back. The bottoms and tops of bedposts, he added, could be used in the same way.

A hollow could hardly be found by tapping, the Prefect replied, if a wad of cotton had been packed around the hidden object, and in any case the search had to be carried out in silence. His men therefore examined the rungs of every chair in the hotel, and the joints of every other piece of furniture, with a most powerful microscope. A single grain of fresh sawdust would have been as obvious to them as an apple, and any gap in the glue would have given the secret away.

I supposed that the mirrors had been examined between the glass and the backing, and that the beds and bedclothes had been probed, together with the curtains and carpets. Of course, said the Prefect, with the weary patience of a man whose methods are questioned by amateurs. When every particle of the furniture had been completed in this way, he added, his men had begun on the house itself.

The whole surface of the building, the Prefect said, had been divided into numbered compartments so that no portion could be forgotten, and each square inch had then been scrutinised with the microscope as before. This included the two houses immediately next door, which I thought an astonishing labour. It was a great deal of trouble, he admitted, but the reward on offer was prodigious.

All the grounds were paved with brick, the Prefect told us, and they gave his men comparatively little trouble, since they had only to examine the moss between the bricks, and they found it untouched. Had a letter been buried there, the disturbance would have shown even to a careless eye. It was a small satisfaction in a search that was proving long and fruitless.

Every package and parcel in the house had been opened, the Prefect continued, and every book had been taken apart leaf by leaf, not merely shaken, as some police officers are content to do. The thickness of each cover was measured with the most accurate care and examined under the microscope, in case the binding had been tampered with. Five or six volumes, fresh from the binder, were also probed lengthwise with the needles.

Every carpet had been taken up and the boards beneath studied with the microscope, he said, and the paper on the walls had been examined in the same way, and the cellars had been searched as well. To each of my questions he gave the same weary yes, and I began to see that the police had been thorough almost beyond belief. I concluded that my own first guess had been right, and that the letter could not be in the house at all.

The Prefect agreed that I was probably right, and he asked Dupin what he would advise, but the answer was only a thorough second search of the premises. The Prefect dismissed this as absolutely needless, for he was no surer that he breathed than that the letter was not in the hotel. He then read out a minute description of the missing paper from his notebook, and departed more depressed in spirits than I had ever known him.

About a month later he paid us another visit and found us occupied very much as before, and when I asked about the purloined letter he answered in the angriest of tones. He had made the second search as Dupin had suggested, he said, but it had been labour lost, as he had known it would be. The reward had lately been doubled, he added, though even a threefold increase would not have let him do more than he had done.

Dupin, drawling between puffs of his meerschaum, suggested that the Prefect had not exerted himself to the utmost, and that he might do a little more by taking counsel in the matter. To illustrate, he told a story of the famous physician Abernethy, to whom a rich miser once described his own symptoms as those of an imaginary person, hoping to win a free medical opinion. The doctor, naturally enough, told him to take advice, and that was the whole of the joke.

The Prefect, a little disconcerted, replied that he was perfectly willing to take advice and to pay for it, and that he would give fifty thousand francs to anyone who could help him. In that case, said Dupin, opening a drawer and taking out a cheque book, he might as well write a cheque for that sum, and the letter would be handed over as soon as it was signed. I was astounded, and the Prefect sat for some minutes speechless and motionless, staring at my friend with his mouth open.

At length, after several pauses and vacant stares, the Prefect seized a pen and wrote out a cheque for fifty thousand francs, which Dupin examined with care and placed in his pocket-book. Then Dupin unlocked a desk, took out a letter, and handed it over, and the Prefect grasped it in an agony of joy and tore it open with a trembling hand. After one rapid glance at its contents he scrambled to the door and rushed from the room and the house without uttering a syllable.

When the Prefect had gone, my friend began his explanation by saying that the Parisian police were exceedingly able in their way, persevering, ingenious and thoroughly versed in the knowledge their duties demand. Had the letter been hidden anywhere within the range of their search, he said, they would unquestionably have found it. Their defect lay not in their measures, which were excellent of their kind, but in the fact that those measures were quite unsuited to the case and to the man.

The Prefect, Dupin continued, was always too deep or too shallow for the matter in hand, and many a schoolboy was a better reasoner than he. He had known one, perhaps eight years old, whose success at the game of even and odd had won universal admiration. In this game one player hides marbles in his fist and the other guesses whether their number is even or odd, and that boy had won every marble in his school.

Of course the boy had a principle, said Dupin, and it lay in judging the cleverness of his opponent. Against a simpleton who had held an even number the first time, he reasoned that the fellow's cunning would just be enough to switch to odd, and so he guessed odd and won. Against a slightly cleverer player he reasoned that a simple switch would seem too obvious, so the opponent would keep to even, and again he won.

I remarked that this was merely an identification of the reasoner's intellect with that of his opponent, and Dupin agreed with satisfaction. When he asked the boy how he managed it, the child said he shaped his face exactly like his opponent's and waited to see what thoughts arose in his own mind to match it. That simple practice, said Dupin, lay behind much of what the world has taken for profound wisdom.

The police fail, Dupin explained, because they never put themselves in the mind of the person they are hunting, and consider only their own ideas of ingenuity. In searching for anything hidden, they think only of the places where they would have hidden it themselves, which serves them well against ordinary minds but fails against a different kind. When driven by some great reward, they merely exaggerate their old methods, without ever questioning the principles behind them.

The remote source of the Prefect's defeat, Dupin said, was his belief that the Minister must be a fool because he had won fame as a poet. All fools are poets, the Prefect feels, and from this he wrongly concludes that all poets are fools. When I objected that the Minister was a mathematician who had written learnedly on the calculus, Dupin replied that he was both, and that a mere mathematician could not have reasoned at all.

Dupin had known the Minister as a courtier and a bold schemer, a man who could not fail to understand the ordinary methods of the police. His frequent absences at night, which the Prefect had welcomed as a gift, Dupin took to be ruses, meant to give the searchers every chance and so convince them that the letter was not there. Such a man, he reasoned, would despise every ordinary hiding place, and would be driven to simplicity if he did not choose it deliberately.

Dupin reminded me how desperately the Prefect had laughed when he suggested, at their first meeting, that the mystery might trouble the police because it was so very self-evident. Full of these ideas, Dupin said, he prepared himself with a pair of green spectacles and called one fine morning, apparently quite by accident, at the Minister's hotel. I could not decide whether he was more amused or more excited by the little drama that he had planned.

Dupin said that he found the Minister at home, yawning, lounging and dawdling as usual, and pretending to be utterly bored, although he was perhaps the most energetic man alive when nobody was watching. To be even with him, Dupin complained of his weak eyes and of the unhappy necessity of wearing spectacles. Under their cover he surveyed the whole apartment with the greatest care, while seeming to attend only to the conversation of his host.

Dupin paid particular attention to a large writing-table near which the Minister sat, and upon which lay, in some confusion, letters and papers, with one or two musical instruments and a few books. After a long and very deliberate scrutiny he could see nothing there to excite the faintest suspicion, and he began to wonder whether the Minister was as clever as he had supposed. A less careful watcher might have stopped there, but Dupin let his eyes move slowly around the rest of the room.

At length Dupin's eyes, going round the room, fell upon a cheap card-rack of pasteboard that hung dangling by a dirty blue ribbon from a small brass knob just beneath the middle of the mantelpiece. In its compartments were five or six visiting cards and a single letter, much soiled and crumpled, and torn almost in two, as if its owner had meant to destroy it but changed his mind. It had been thrust carelessly, even contemptuously, into one of the upper divisions of the rack, in full view of anyone who cared to look.

Dupin concluded at once that this was the letter he sought, although in appearance it was radically different from the description the Prefect had read out. Its seal was large and black, with the Minister's own cipher, whereas the stolen letter had a small red seal bearing the arms of a noble family. The address, too, was to the Minister himself, in a small feminine hand instead of the bold writing of a royal personage, and only the size of the two agreed.

Yet the very extremity of these differences, together with the dirt and the torn condition of the paper, seemed to Dupin quite wrong for so methodical a man as the Minister. They suggested a plan to persuade any visitor that the letter was worthless, and its position in full view of everyone only strengthened his suspicion. He prolonged his visit as long as he could, and kept the Minister in animated talk on a subject that never failed to excite him, while his attention stayed riveted on the letter.

Scrutinising the edges, Dupin saw that they were more chafed than seemed necessary, with the broken look of stiff paper that has been folded again the opposite way along its old creases. That discovery set his last doubts at rest, for it was clear that the letter had been turned inside out like a glove, readdressed and resealed. He wished the Minister good morning and departed at once, leaving a gold snuff-box on the table.

Dupin returned next morning for his snuff-box, and the two men resumed their conversation of the day before with great eagerness. While they were thus engaged, a loud report, as of a pistol, rang out immediately beneath the windows, followed by a series of fearful screams and the shouting of a terrified mob. The Minister rushed to a casement, threw it open, and leaned out to see what had happened in the street below.

In the meantime, Dupin said, he stepped quietly to the card-rack, took the letter, and slipped it into his pocket. In its place he left a facsimile, so far as outward appearance went, which he had carefully prepared at his lodgings, imitating the Minister's cipher very readily with a seal made of bread. The whole exchange took only a few seconds, and his host's back was turned to him throughout.

The disturbance in the street, Dupin explained, had been caused by the frantic behaviour of a man with a musket, who had fired it into a crowd, though it proved to be loaded without a ball. The fellow was allowed to go his way as a lunatic or a drunkard, and the Minister turned back from the window just as Dupin, who had secured what he wanted, stepped away from the rack. In fact the pretended madman was a man in Dupin's own pay, hired for the occasion.

I asked what purpose Dupin had had in replacing the letter with a copy, and whether it would not have been better to seize it openly at the first visit and depart. The Minister, he replied, was a desperate man and a man of nerve, and his hotel was full of attendants devoted to his interests. Had Dupin made the wild attempt I suggested, he might never have left the ministerial presence alive, and the good people of Paris would have heard of him no more.

There was a second reason, Dupin said, for in this matter he was the partisan of the lady concerned. For eighteen months the Minister had held her in his power, but now she held him in hers, since he did not know that the letter was gone and would go on making his demands as before. In doing so he would inevitably commit himself, all at once, to his own political destruction, and it would be no gentle fall.

His downfall, Dupin added, would be no less awkward than sudden, for in every kind of climbing it is far easier to get up than to come down. For the man who descended he had no sympathy and no pity, since the Minister was that monstrous creature, an unprincipled man of genius. I could see that the contest had become, for my friend, a matter of principle as well as of skill.

Dupin confessed that he would very much like to know the precise character of the Minister's thoughts when the lady defied him and he was reduced to opening the letter left in the card-rack. I asked at once whether he had put anything in particular inside it, for it seemed to me that he must have. My friend smiled over his pipe, as though he had been waiting for the question.

It did not seem altogether right, Dupin said, to leave the inside of the letter blank, for that would have been insulting. The Minister had once done him an evil turn in Vienna, which Dupin had promised, quite good-humouredly, to remember. It seemed a pity not to give him a clue, for he knew Dupin's handwriting well, and a few words copied into the middle of the empty sheet would tell him who had outwitted him.

The words, Dupin said, were two lines from Crébillon's tragedy Atrée, and they mean in effect that a design so deadly, if it is not worthy of Atreus, is worthy of his brother Thyestes. The Minister would know the handwriting at once, and he would understand who had outwitted him, and why. It was, I thought, the neatest signature that any thief-catcher ever left behind him, and it was written in a hand the Minister could not mistake.

So ended the affair of the purloined letter, which the Prefect's needles and microscopes had failed to find in months of patient labour, and which a single morning's visit by Dupin had placed in his hands. The paper had lain in plain view all the while, safest precisely because no man of the Prefect's kind would think of looking where everyone could see. It was a fitting end to a tale in which the best hiding place proved to be the most obvious one of all.
